claim: Embryogenesis is an essential and stereotypic process that nevertheless evolves among species.
source: Embryogenesis is an essential and stereotypic process that nevertheless evolves among species.
evidence: This is a general statement about embryogenesis presented in the abstract without specific experimental data from this manuscript, but draws on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The essentiality of embryogenesis may favor the accumulation of cryptic genetic variation (CGV) that has no effect in the wild-type but that enhances or suppresses the effects of rare disruptions to gene function.
source: Its essentiality may favor the accumulation of cryptic genetic variation (CGV) that has no effect in the wild-type but that enhances or suppresses the effects of rare disruptions to gene function.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the potential evolutionary consequences of essentiality, representing speculation about mechanisms.

claim: Each perturbation of maternal-effect genes revealed cryptic genetic variation in C. elegans wild strains.
source: Each perturbation revealed CGV, indicating that wild-type genomes harbor myriad genetic modifiers that may have little effect individually but which in aggregate can dramatically influence penetrance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results showing variation in embryonic lethality across strains and gene perturbations.

claim: Wild-type C. elegans genomes harbor myriad genetic modifiers that may have little effect individually but which in aggregate can dramatically influence penetrance.
source: Each perturbation revealed CGV, indicating that wild-type genomes harbor myriad genetic modifiers that may have little effect individually but which in aggregate can dramatically influence penetrance.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that each perturbation revealed CGV and the statistical analysis showing polygenic effects.

claim: Embryonic lethality phenotypes were mediated by many modifiers, indicating high polygenicity.
source: Phenotypes were mediated by many modifiers, indicating high polygenicity, but the alleles tend to act very specifically, indicating low pleiotropy.
evidence: This is supported by the genomic heritability estimates and the observation that genetic similarity among strains explained phenotypic similarity for most perturbations.

claim: The modifier alleles tend to act very specifically, indicating low pleiotropy.
source: Phenotypes were mediated by many modifiers, indicating high polygenicity, but the alleles tend to act very specifically, indicating low pleiotropy.
evidence: This is supported by the low correlations between gene perturbations and the discrete nature of genotype-phenotype associations in GWAS.

claim: The effect of gene disruption on an organism depends on a combination of the gene's function and the genetic background in which it resides.
source: The effect of gene disruption on an organism depends on a combination of the gene's function and the genetic background in which it resides (Chandler et al., 2013; Chari and Dworkin, 2013; Vu et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The average human genome contains loss-of-function alleles for 100 or more genes.
source: The average human genome contains loss-of-function alleles for 100 or more genes, some of which cause known genetic diseases (Abecasis et al., 2010; MacArthur et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous genomic studies.

claim: Disease expression depends on exposure of the disease allele and on variants elsewhere in the genome that act as penetrance modifiers.
source: disease expression depends on exposure of the disease allele, such as by homozygosity, but also on variants elsewhere in the genome that act as penetrance modifiers (Hamilton and Yu, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on genetic disease.

claim: Genetic background effects are an example of cryptic genetic variation (CGV).
source: Genetic background effects are an example of cryptic genetic variation (CGV), the class of mutations that affect phenotype under rare conditions (Gibson and Dworkin, 2004; Paaby and Rockman, 2014).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: CGV is invisible until a perturbation changes the molecular, cellular, or developmental processes that govern its phenotypic expression.
source: CGV is invisible until a perturbation changes the molecular, cellular, or developmental processes that govern its phenotypic expression.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about CGV based on established knowledge.

claim: CGV may be 'released' by environmental exposure, like modern changes to diet that have been hypothesized to underlie the emergence of complex metabolic diseases in humans.
source: In addition to genetic perturbations, CGV may be 'released' by environmental exposure, like the modern changes to diet that have been hypothesized to underlie the emergence of complex metabolic diseases in humans (Gibson, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on environmental effects on CGV.

claim: The concept of CGV has been of longstanding interest to evolutionary theorists because it explains how populations might store alleles that enable adaptation when conditions change.
source: The concept of CGV has been of longstanding interest to evolutionary theorists because it explains how populations might store alleles that enable adaptation when conditions change (Dobzhansky, 1941; Waddington, 1956; McGuigan et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to evolutionary theory literature.

claim: Inhibition of the heat shock chaperone protein HSP90 reveals previously-silent mutational effects across many taxa.
source: Most of our empirical knowledge of CGV arises from studies that inhibited the heat shock chaperone protein HSP90 to reveal previously-silent mutational effects across many taxa, which probably represents a general mechanism that buffers genome-wide functional variation (Queitsch et al., 2002; Yeyati et al., 2007; Jarosz and Lindquist, 2010; Chen and Wagner, 2012; Rohner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to HSP90 studies.

claim: HSP90 probably represents a general mechanism that buffers genome-wide functional variation.
source: Most of our empirical knowledge of CGV arises from studies that inhibited the heat shock chaperone protein HSP90 to reveal previously-silent mutational effects across many taxa, which probably represents a general mechanism that buffers genome-wide functional variation (Queitsch et al., 2002; Yeyati et al., 2007; Jarosz and Lindquist, 2010; Chen and Wagner, 2012; Rohner et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited studies, with speculative language ('probably').

claim: C. elegans embryogenesis is both complex and typically invariant.
source: C. elegans embryogenesis is both complex and typically invariant, which may favor the accumulation of mutations that act in a conditionally-functional manner (Gibson and Dworkin, 2004; Paaby and Rockman, 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about C. elegans embryogenesis based on established knowledge.

claim: The complexity and invariance of C. elegans embryogenesis may favor the accumulation of mutations that act in a conditionally-functional manner.
source: C. elegans embryogenesis is both complex and typically invariant, which may favor the accumulation of mutations that act in a conditionally-functional manner (Gibson and Dworkin, 2004; Paaby and Rockman, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about evolutionary consequences, supported by citations.

claim: 29 maternal-effect genes were individually targeted in each of 55 wild C. elegans strains from around the globe.
source: To uncover the nature and extent of natural genetic modifiers in C. elegans embryogenesis, we individually targeted 29 maternal-effect genes in each of 55 wild strains from around the globe (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: RNAi was delivered by feeding the parental generation Escherichia coli expressing dsRNA against the target genes.
source: RNAi was delivered by feeding the parental generation Escherichia coli expressing dsRNA against the target genes (Cipriani and Piano, 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental method used.

claim: Each combination of strain and targeted gene was replicated in at least eight wells.
source: Each combination of strain and targeted gene was replicated in at least eight wells, and within each well an average of 10 adult worms contributed hundreds of offspring that were screened as dead or alive.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and replication.

claim: Within each well an average of 10 adult worms contributed hundreds of offspring that were screened as dead or alive.
source: Each combination of strain and targeted gene was replicated in at least eight wells, and within each well an average of 10 adult worms contributed hundreds of offspring that were screened as dead or alive.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Estimates of embryonic lethality were extracted by the image analysis algorithm DevStaR.
source: Estimates of embryonic lethality were extracted by the image analysis algorithm DevStaR, which was developed to recognize C. elegans developmental stages for this specific application (White et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the data analysis method used.

claim: DevStaR was developed to recognize C. elegans developmental stages for this specific application.
source: Estimates of embryonic lethality were extracted by the image analysis algorithm DevStaR, which was developed to recognize C. elegans developmental stages for this specific application (White et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the DevStaR publication.

claim: The probability that an embryo would fail to develop was modeled as a function of targeted gene, worm strain, strain-by-gene interaction, and several experimental variables.
source: We then modeled the probability that an embryo would fail to develop as a function of targeted gene, worm strain, strain-by-gene interaction, and several experimental variables (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling approach.

claim: The experiments revealed extensive variation in embryonic lethality caused by genetic differences among strains.
source: The experiments revealed extensive variation in embryonic lethality caused by genetic differences among strains (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Substantial variation among strains was observed, with some strains exhibiting more embryonic lethality across all targeted genes than other strains.
source: We observed substantial variation among strains, with some strains exhibiting more embryonic lethality across all targeted genes than other strains, but also significant gene-specific among-strain variation, where particular combinations of gene and strain exhibited surprisingly high or low lethality (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Significant gene-specific among-strain variation was observed, where particular combinations of gene and strain exhibited surprisingly high or low lethality.
source: We observed substantial variation among strains, with some strains exhibiting more embryonic lethality across all targeted genes than other strains, but also significant gene-specific among-strain variation, where particular combinations of gene and strain exhibited surprisingly high or low lethality (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Informational modifiers alter the effect of the initial perturbation in a non-gene-specific manner.
source: Informational modifiers (such as suppressors of nonsense mutations in classical screens [e.g., Hodgkin et al., 1989], and modifiers of germline RNAi sensitivity in this experiment) alter the effect of the initial perturbation in a non-gene-specific manner, while gene-specific modifiers reveal functional features of the targeted locus.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation and inference from the experimental design.

claim: Gene-specific modifiers reveal functional features of the targeted locus.
source: Informational modifiers (such as suppressors of nonsense mutations in classical screens [e.g., Hodgkin et al., 1989], and modifiers of germline RNAi sensitivity in this experiment) alter the effect of the initial perturbation in a non-gene-specific manner, while gene-specific modifiers reveal functional features of the targeted locus.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of gene-specific modifiers.

claim: Half of the variation attributable to heritable modifier variation among worms is explained by non-gene-specific informational modifiers and half by gene-specific modifier effects.
source: Of the variation attributable to heritable modifier variation among worms, half is explained by non-gene-specific informational modifiers and half by gene-specific modifier effects (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: All terms in the statistical model were highly significant, including the strain-by-gene interaction.
source: All terms were highly significant, including the strain-by-gene interaction, which represents variation attributable to cryptic genetic modifiers that act gene-specifically.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The strain-by-gene interaction represents variation attributable to cryptic genetic modifiers that act gene-specifically.
source: All terms were highly significant, including the strain-by-gene interaction, which represents variation attributable to cryptic genetic modifiers that act gene-specifically.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical model term.

claim: The strain term and the strain-by-gene interaction term explain similar amounts of variation and together account for 31% of the total deviance.
source: This term and the strain term, which represents variation attributable to informational modifiers affecting germline RNAi, explain similar amounts of variation, and together account for 31% of the total deviance.
evidence: This is calculated from the statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The strain term represents variation attributable to informational modifiers affecting germline RNAi.
source: This term and the strain term, which represents variation attributable to informational modifiers affecting germline RNAi, explain similar amounts of variation, and together account for 31% of the total deviance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical model term.

claim: The variation in embryonic lethality attributable to informational modifiers provides an estimate of each strain's sensitivity to exogenous germline RNAi.
source: The variation in embryonic lethality attributable to informational modifiers, represented by genetic strain effect in our statistical model, provides an estimate of each strain's sensitivity to exogenous germline RNAi.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical model results.

claim: Dramatic variation in sensitivity to germline RNAi was observed among strains.
source: We observed dramatic variation in sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most strains exhibited moderately reduced lethality penetrance relative to the RNAi-sensitive laboratory strain N2.
source: Most strains exhibited moderately reduced lethality penetrance relative to the RNAi-sensitive laboratory strain N2, but two strains, the germline RNAi-insensitive strain CB4856 (Tijsterman et al., 2002) and the genetically divergent strain QX1211, showed consistently weak penetrance across the targeted genes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CB4856 and QX1211 showed consistently weak penetrance across the targeted genes.
source: Most strains exhibited moderately reduced lethality penetrance relative to the RNAi-sensitive laboratory strain N2, but two strains, the germline RNAi-insensitive strain CB4856 (Tijsterman et al., 2002) and the genetically divergent strain QX1211, showed consistently weak penetrance across the targeted genes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CB4856 harbors a ppw-1 loss-of-function mutation that confers resistance to germline RNAi.
source: CB4856 harbors a ppw-1 loss-of-function mutation that confers resistance to germline RNAi (Tijsterman et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Sequencing shows that QX1211 and other strains with intermediate sensitivity do not have ppw-1 loss-of-function mutations.
source: but sequencing shows that QX1211 and other strains with intermediate sensitivity do not.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data generated in this study.

claim: A ppw-1 mutation in the N2 background was more sensitive than CB4856, showing high lethality on mex-3 and pos-1.
source: We found that a ppw-1 mutation in the N2 background was more sensitive than CB4856, showing high lethality on mex-3 and pos-1 (Figure 2)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some of the difference between N2 and CB4856 in RNAi sensitivity is ppw-1-independent.
source: indicating that some of the difference between N2 and CB4856 is ppw-1-independent.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ppw-1 mutation in N2 background differs from CB4856.

claim: Insensitivity to germline RNAi is genetically complex.
source: These results demonstrate that insensitivity to germline RNAi is genetically complex and that wild C. elegans populations harbor many alleles affecting germline RNAi (Elvin et al., 2011; Pollard and Rockman, 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results showing variation beyond ppw-1.

claim: Wild C. elegans populations harbor many alleles affecting germline RNAi.
source: These results demonstrate that insensitivity to germline RNAi is genetically complex and that wild C. elegans populations harbor many alleles affecting germline RNAi (Elvin et al., 2011; Pollard and Rockman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations to previous work.

claim: Among wild-type strains, all but four (KR314, JU396, CB4852 and ED3040) showed complete sensitivity to somatic RNAi on tba-2.
source: Among wild-type strains, all but four (KR314, JU396, CB4852 and ED3040) showed complete sensitivity to somatic RNAi, indicated by developmental arrest of P0 animals on tba-2
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from tba-2 targeting.

claim: Complete sensitivity to somatic RNAi demonstrates that most wild-type strains take up dsRNA and are capable of RNAi.
source: which demonstrates that most wild-type strains take up dsRNA and are capable of RNAi.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of somatic RNAi sensitivity.

claim: An rrf-1 deletion mutant is sensitive to RNAi against genes expressed in the germline but resistant to RNAi in most somatic tissues.
source: An rrf-1 deletion mutant, which is sensitive to RNAi against genes expressed in the germline but resistant to RNAi in most somatic tissues (Yigit et al., 2006; Kumsta and Hansen, 2012), grew to adulthood but laid dead embryos
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental observation.

claim: The rrf-1 deletion mutant grew to adulthood but laid dead embryos on tba-2 RNAi.
source: An rrf-1 deletion mutant, which is sensitive to RNAi against genes expressed in the germline but resistant to RNAi in most somatic tissues (Yigit et al., 2006; Kumsta and Hansen, 2012), grew to adulthood but laid dead embryos
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Germline RNAi successfully silenced maternal tba-2 required for embryonic development in the rrf-1 mutant.
source: suggesting that germline RNAi successfully silenced maternal tba-2 required for embryonic development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rrf-1 mutants laid dead embryos.

claim: The four somatically-resistant wild strains exhibited embryonic lethality on tba-2 and other germline-expressed genes.
source: The four somatically-resistant wild strains also exhibited embryonic lethality on tba-2 and other germline-expressed genes, confirming that the modifier variability acts tissue-specifically.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The modifier variability acts tissue-specifically.
source: The four somatically-resistant wild strains also exhibited embryonic lethality on tba-2 and other germline-expressed genes, confirming that the modifier variability acts tissue-specifically.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential sensitivity to somatic vs. germline RNAi.

claim: Gene-specific modifiers explain as much of the total variation as the informational modifiers.
source: Gene-specific modifiers explain as much of the total variation as the informational modifiers, as estimated by the strain-by-gene interaction term in our model (Table 1), and represent cryptic genetic variation in developmental processes.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Gene-specific modifiers represent cryptic genetic variation in developmental processes.
source: Gene-specific modifiers explain as much of the total variation as the informational modifiers, as estimated by the strain-by-gene interaction term in our model (Table 1), and represent cryptic genetic variation in developmental processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: Gene-specific modifiers could act via network bypasses, where loss of the targeted gene reveals variation among strains in developmental network structure.
source: The modifiers could act via network bypasses, where loss of the targeted gene reveals variation among strains in developmental network structure (e.g., Zhang and Emmons, 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Gene-specific modifiers could act on the extent of the knockdown at a gene-specific level, resulting in variable residual activity of the targeted gene.
source: Gene-specific modifiers could also act on the extent of the knockdown at a gene-specific level, in a manner akin to intragenic suppressors, resulting in variable residual activity of the targeted gene.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Each of the 29 genes targeted showed significant strain-by-gene interaction coefficients.
source: Each of the 29 genes we targeted showed significant strain-by-gene interaction coefficients, indicating that genetic modifiers of embryonic gene perturbations are pervasive in natural populations.

claim: Genetic modifiers of embryonic gene perturbations are pervasive in natural populations.
source: Each of the 29 genes we targeted showed significant strain-by-gene interaction coefficients, indicating that genetic modifiers of embryonic gene perturbations are pervasive in natural populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all 29 genes showed significant interaction coefficients.

claim: 36 gene pairs have known physical or genetic interactions.
source: 36 gene pairs have known physical or genetic interactions, but these did not show significantly elevated phenotypic correlations (χ2 = 2.30, df = 1, p = 0.13).

claim: Gene pairs with known physical or genetic interactions did not show significantly elevated phenotypic correlations.
source: 36 gene pairs have known physical or genetic interactions, but these did not show significantly elevated phenotypic correlations (χ2 = 2.30, df = 1, p = 0.13).

claim: The average pairwise par gene correlation was no higher than the average correlation across all genes.
source: For example, despite high interaction within the par network, which underlies polarization of the zygote, the average pairwise par gene correlation was no higher than the average correlation across all genes (Supplementary file 1).

source: Coefficients for par-3 and par-6 were correlated (correlation = 0.40, p = 0.003)

claim: Redundancy allows shared function of some factors and specificity of others.

claim: Over evolutionary time, purifying selection should deplete populations of pleiotropic alleles as they may be more likely to be deleterious.

source: We found that for most of the perturbations, variation in lethality penetrance is due to common alleles at many contributing cryptic loci.

claim: Variants with effects under one perturbation have no detectable effects under another.

claim: Modifier phenotypes for pkc-3 and rfc-3 are associated with SNPs on both chromosome III and X.
source: Separately, modifier phenotypes for pkc-3, involved in anterior-posterior polarity in the early embryo, and rfc-3, which shows homology to DNA replication factors C and effects on cell cycle synchrony (Piano et al., 2002), are associated with SNPs on both chromosome III and X.

claim: pkc-3 is involved in anterior-posterior polarity in the early embryo.

source: Because the co-associations occur twice, with unlinked SNPs (R2 = 0.26), they implicate the presence of at least two interacting cryptic alleles and provide independent lines of evidence for a relationship between pkc-3 and rfc-3, genes with no reported interactions or shared functions.

claim: The co-associations provide independent lines of evidence for a relationship between pkc-3 and rfc-3, genes with no reported interactions or shared functions.

claim: Pervasive CGV was uncovered that modifies the probability that an embryo will survive a gene perturbation.
source: We have uncovered pervasive CGV that modifies the probability that an embryo will survive a gene perturbation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the experimental data.

claim: By evaluating the effects of naturally-occurring mutations on gene knockdowns, this study explored a genotypic space that is distinct from that accessible to conventional screens.
source: By evaluating the effects of naturally-occurring mutations on gene knockdowns, we explored a genotypic space that is distinct from that accessible to conventional screens.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The findings provide complementary insight, including discovery of modifier activity that may be detectable only when effects are moderate or polygenic.
source: Our findings provide complementary insight, including discovery of modifier activity that may be detectable only when effects are moderate (Fievet et al., 2013) or polygenic (Mackay, 2014).

claim: The variation is described as 'cryptic' because its effect on embryonic survival is dramatically magnified under perturbed conditions.
source: We describe the variation we uncovered as 'cryptic' because its effect on embryonic survival is dramatically magnified under perturbed conditions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about the nature of the variation observed.

claim: Without gene perturbation, the strains exhibit little embryonic lethality.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms.

claim: Whether a genetic variant is cryptic requires definition of the focal phenotype, since even at the morphological level an allele can be cryptic in one trait but penetrant in another.
source: whether a genetic variant is cryptic requires definition of the focal phenotype, since even at the morphological level an allele can be cryptic in one trait but penetrant in another (Duveau and Félix, 2012).

claim: CGV has been demonstrated following perturbation of candidate genes.

claim: The potential role of CGV in adaptive evolution has been considered in diverse systems.

claim: By systematic evaluation, the phenomenon of conditionally functional variation pervades even the highly stereotyped and controlled process of embryogenesis.
source: Here, we show by systematic evaluation that the phenomenon of conditionally functional variation pervades even the highly stereotyped and controlled process of embryogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Wild populations harbor many enhancers and suppressors of critical embryonic genes.
source: We found that gene-specific cryptic variation affects every targeted gene, implying that wild populations harbor many enhancers and suppressors of critical embryonic genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all 29 genes showed significant strain-by-gene interactions.

claim: In humans, penetrance modifiers may mediate expression of genetic diseases arising from loss-of-function mutations.
source: In humans, such penetrance modifiers may mediate expression of genetic diseases arising from loss-of-function mutations (Abecasis et al., 2010; Hamilton and Yu, 2012; MacArthur et al., 2012)
evidence: This is a speculative statement about human disease supported by citations.

claim: If the crypsis of penetrance modifiers is environmentally influenced, they may also explain modern disease susceptibility.
source: and if their crypsis is environmentally influenced they may also explain modern disease susceptibility (Gibson, 2009).

claim: The screen revealed dramatic variation among wild-type strains in their responses to exogenous RNAi in the germline.
source: Our screen also revealed dramatic variation among wild-type strains in their responses to exogenous RNAi in the germline.

claim: Somatic RNAi response has been shown to influence C. elegans susceptibility to viral infection.
source: Somatic RNAi response has been shown to influence C. elegans susceptibility to viral infection

claim: Conditionally-functional relationships between genes may pervade the variation on which natural selection acts, affecting how complex traits evolve.
source: The variation we describe illustrates how conditionally-functional relationships between genes may pervade the variation on which natural selection acts, affecting how complex traits evolve (True and Haag, 2001; Félix, 2007; Wang and Sommer, 2011; Verster et al., 2014) and the nature of their genetic architecture (Mackay, 2014).
